chapters.title: A Letter to God
chapters.summary: A Letter to God, a story by Gregorio Lopez y Fuentes, describes how a poor farmer's faith survives disaster. When a hailstorm destroys his ripe corn, Lencho writes a letter to God asking for a hundred pesos. The kind postmaster secretly sends him seventy pesos, and Lencho's furious reply to God creates the story's famous irony.
hotTopics: Lencho's unshaken faith in God
The hailstorm that destroyed the crop
The postmaster's act of charity
The irony of the second letter
Extract-based questions on the rain-as-coins lines
Value angle: faith, gratitude and kindness

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: Lencho, a hardworking and God-fearing farmer, lived in the only house in the entire valley, on the crest of a low hill, overlooking a field of ripe corn dotted with flowers that promised a good harvest.
The field needed only a downpour; when rain finally fell, a delighted Lencho compared the big drops to ten-cent coins and the smaller ones to fives, calling them new silver coins.
Suddenly a strong wind began to blow and huge hailstones fell for a full hour, covering the field like salt; not a flower or leaf survived, the trees stood bare, and the entire corn was destroyed.
Grieving but resolute, Lencho wrote a letter to God asking for a hundred pesos to sow the field again and to live until the new crop, and posted it addressed simply to God.

The postman showed the letter to the postmaster, who laughed at first but then collected seventy pesos from the employees and friends, adding part of his own salary, and mailed it signed with the single word God.

Lencho, not at all surprised but angry at finding only seventy pesos, wrote a second letter asking God to send the remaining thirty, but not through the mail, because the post office employees were a bunch of crooks.

keyTerms.meaning: a poor, God-fearing farmer whose crop is destroyed by hail
a storm of falling ice that ruins the cornfield
the currency in which Lencho asks God for help
Lencho's way of seeking divine help, posted in the mailbox
the amiable official who collects money to reply to Lencho
Lencho's unfair label for the post office employees

sections.trick: Remember the four beats in order: Corn ripe, Hail falls, Postmaster pays, Crooks blamed - C-H-P-C tells the whole story.
sections.examPointer: Two-mark favourites are why Lencho wrote to God and how the postmaster reacted; the irony of the second letter is the most repeated three and five mark angle.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: Unwavering faith in God: Lencho's absolute, almost childlike trust that God sees everything and will answer his letter exactly as asked.
Human kindness and charity: the postmaster's quiet decision to protect a stranger's faith by collecting money without taking credit.
Irony: the very people who collected the money are accused of being crooks, showing how blind faith can be unfair to human helpers.
Hope and resilience in hardship: the farmer does not give up even after total loss, but seeks a solution at once.
Message: faith gives strength to face loss, but it must be balanced with gratitude and reason; anonymous goodness asks for no thanks.

keyTerms.meaning: complete trust in God without needing proof
Lencho's belief that his loss can be repaired
the postmaster's selfless act of raising money for Lencho
the contrast between what Lencho expects and the truth that his helpers collected the money
Lencho's childlike simplicity and naivety
the value the story quietly demands but Lencho fails to show

sections.trick: F-C-I-G: Faith, Charity, Irony, Gratitude - the four theme words that should appear in any long answer.
sections.examPointer: Value-based questions almost always test faith versus kindness; always mention that the postmaster is the real face of God in the story.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: Lencho is an ox of a man, working like an animal in the fields, yet he knows how to write; he is simple, honest and deeply religious.
Lencho's faith is unshaken: he believes God can neither make a mistake nor refuse what is asked, and he shows no surprise at receiving the money.
Lencho is also naive and quick to suspect: without any proof he brands the post office employees a bunch of crooks in his second letter.
The postmaster is a fat, amiable fellow who laughs at the letter first, then takes it seriously and acts with rare generosity.
The postmaster's kindness is practical: he gives part of his own salary and gathers contributions purely to keep a stranger's faith in God alive.
The postman is the amused carrier who brings the letter addressed to God to the postmaster's notice.

keyTerms.meaning: an ox of a man; hardworking, honest, deeply religious yet naive
fat and amiable; humorous at first, generous in the end
the amused letter carrier who reports the letter to the postmaster
the contributors to the charity whom Lencho wrongly accuses
the unseen addressee of both letters, representing absolute faith

sections.trick: Contrast pair: Lencho = faith without sight; Postmaster = faith in humanity - quote both traits with one example each.
sections.examPointer: Character sketch of Lencho or the postmaster is a regular five-mark LA; support every trait with one textual incident to score full marks.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: Learn CBSE-style meanings of the chapter's vocabulary; one word is usually tested in extract-based or one-mark style items.
Group the words by scene: farm words (crest, downpour, hailstone) and post office words (amiable, resolved).
Phrases like an ox of a man and a bunch of crooks are idioms; explain them in a line, not literally.
Use each word in a sentence from the story context to retain it longer.
Revise spellings of these terms before the exam since they recur in answers.

keyTerms.meaning: the top of a low hill where Lencho's house stood
a heavy fall of rain that Lencho awaited for his crop
a pellet of falling ice that destroyed the entire crop
friendly and good-natured, as the postmaster is described
firmly determined; the postmaster stuck to his resolution to help
a man who toils like an ox; said of Lencho

sections.trick: C-D-H-A-R: Crest, Downpour, Hailstone, Amiable, Resolved - the five dictionary words examiners love from this chapter.
sections.examPointer: Match meanings with context; writing 'crest' as just 'top' scores less than 'the top of the hill where Lencho's house stood'.

sections.heading: Exam Focus
points: Value-based angle: faith should move mountains, but the story also warns against blind faith that forgets human kindness and gratitude.
Irony is the examiner's favourite device here: Lencho thanks God for sending money yet calls the helpers crooks; practise explaining both sides.
Extract-based questions usually come from the raindrops-as-coins paragraph, the hailstorm description, or the final letter; quote the context accurately.
Short questions often ask why Lencho wrote to God, how the postmaster reacted, why Lencho was angry, and the traits of the postmaster.
For long answers, always link each plot event to a theme (faith, generosity, irony) and close with the message of the story.

keyTerms.meaning: a question based on a quoted passage from the text
an answer linking the story to faith, charity and gratitude
the central literary device tested from this chapter
short answer worth 2 or 3 marks, about 40-80 words
long answer worth 5 marks, about 100-150 words with theme linkage
a trait-based description supported by textual examples

sections.trick: Quote once per answer: one short line from the text (like the bunch of crooks line) instantly strengthens any SA or LA.
sections.examPointer: When asked 'Was Lencho right to call the employees crooks?', always answer No, and prove it with the postmaster's donation before adding the value point.

mcqs.question: What was Lencho's occupation?
mcqs.explanation: Lencho was a hardworking farmer whose entire hope lay in his field of ripe corn.

mcqs.question: Where was Lencho's house located?
options: In the middle of the village square
On the crest of a low hill in the valley
mcqs.explanation: The text says Lencho's house was the only one in the entire valley, standing on the crest of a low hill.

mcqs.question: What did the field of ripe corn dotted with the flowers promise?
mcqs.explanation: Lencho was sure the flowers dotted over the corn promised a good harvest.

mcqs.question: How much money did Lencho ask God to send him?
mcqs.explanation: In his first letter Lencho requested a hundred pesos to sow his field again and to live until the new crop came.

mcqs.question: "The falling raindrops looked, to Lencho, like little new silver coins - the biggest ones like ten-cent pieces and the little ones like fives." What does this comparison reveal about Lencho?
options: He collected silver coins as a hobby
He saw money literally raining down
He saw his hoped-for prosperity in the falling rain
mcqs.explanation: The hopeful farmer linked the rain directly with his harvest and earnings; the simile shows his joy at the coming rain.

mcqs.question: What destroyed Lencho's crop?
options: A hailstorm that lasted an hour
mcqs.explanation: A strong wind brought huge hailstones that fell for an hour, covering the field like salt and destroying the whole crop.

mcqs.question: Who laughed at Lencho's letter first and then took it seriously?
mcqs.explanation: The postmaster first laughed at a letter addressed to God but then resolved to protect Lencho's faith and arranged a reply with money.

mcqs.question: How much money did Lencho actually receive, and how did he react?
options: Seventy pesos; he was happy and thanked God
Seventy pesos; he became angry and called the post office employees a bunch of crooks
A hundred pesos; he was satisfied
Fifty pesos; he politely asked for the rest
mcqs.explanation: The postmaster could gather only seventy pesos; Lencho, blaming the post office staff, demanded the remaining thirty in a second letter.

mcqs.question: "Lencho showed not the slightest surprise on seeing the bills - such was his confidence - but he became angry when he counted the money." What does this line reveal?
options: Lencho did not know how to count money
Lencho was never surprised because his faith in God was absolute
Lencho did not like paper currency
Lencho suspected the bills were fake
mcqs.explanation: His lack of surprise shows his unshaken confidence that God would answer him; the anger shows how he misjudged his human helpers.

mcqs.question: The central irony of the story is that:
options: God really wrote back to Lencho
The people whom Lencho called a bunch of crooks were the very ones who collected money for him
The postmaster kept the money for himself
mcqs.explanation: The postmaster and his staff donated the money, yet Lencho thanked God and abused them, creating the famous ironic twist.

boardQuestions.question: Why did Lencho write a letter to God?
boardQuestions.answer: After the hailstorm destroyed his ripe corn completely, Lencho faced hunger for the whole year. Being a firm believer, he felt that God alone could see his plight and would not let his family starve, so he wrote asking for a hundred pesos to sow the field again and to live until the new crop came.

boardQuestions.question: How did the postmaster react when he first read Lencho's letter?
boardQuestions.answer: The postman brought the letter to the postmaster and both laughed at a letter addressed to God. But the postmaster soon admired the writer's faith, saying he wished he had such confidence, and he resolved to reply to the letter so that Lencho's faith in God should not be shaken.

boardQuestions.question: Describe how the hailstorm destroyed Lencho's field and how Lencho reacted to the disaster.
boardQuestions.answer: As Lencho waited for the rain his corn needed, a strong wind began to blow and huge hailstones fell for a full hour. The field looked as if it were covered with salt; not a flower or a leaf survived, and even the trees stood stripped bare. Lencho's soul was filled with sadness; he felt a plague of locusts would have left more than this, and he feared his family would go hungry that year.

boardQuestions.question: How did the postmaster arrange the money for Lencho, and why did he do it?
boardQuestions.answer: The postmaster decided to answer the letter so that Lencho's faith in God would not be shaken. He stuck to his resolution and asked the post office employees to contribute money for an act of charity, gave a part of his own salary himself, and managed to collect seventy pesos, which he placed in an envelope addressed to Lencho and signed with a single word, God.

boardQuestions.question: Draw a character sketch of Lencho, the farmer in A Letter to God.
boardQuestions.answer: Lencho is a simple, hardworking farmer, an ox of a man who works like an animal in the fields yet knows how to write. He is deeply religious, with absolute, almost childlike faith in God, believing that God sees everything and can neither make a mistake nor refuse what is asked. When his crop is destroyed by hail, he does not despair but acts with hope, writing directly to God for a hundred pesos. However, his faith is blind rather than wise: he shows no surprise at the money, blames the post office employees as a bunch of crooks without any proof, and suspects the very hands that helped him. Thus Lencho is a blend of honesty, hope and naive simplicity.

boardQuestions.question: 'Faith can move mountains, but it must be accompanied by gratitude.' Discuss this statement with reference to the story, focusing on the postmaster's generosity and the irony of the ending.
boardQuestions.answer: Lencho's faith is absolute: seeing his corn destroyed, he writes to God without doubt and waits with the confidence of a believer. The postmaster is so moved that he collects seventy pesos, giving part of his own salary, purely to preserve a stranger's faith in God. Yet the ending is deeply ironic: Lencho thanks God for the money but, finding only seventy pesos, calls the post office employees a bunch of crooks and asks God to send the rest by another route. The human kindness behind the miracle goes unrecognised. The story thus teaches that faith gives strength to endure loss, but blind faith without gratitude and reason can insult the very goodness that sustains us.

boardQuestions.question: "God, if you don't help me, my family and I will go hungry this year. I need a hundred pesos in order to sow my field again and to live until the crop comes." Answer the questions that follow: (a) Why did Lencho need the money, and why did he address his letter to God? (b) How did the postmaster respond to this letter? (c) What reply did Lencho send after receiving the money, and what irony does it create?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) Lencho needed a hundred pesos because the hailstorm had destroyed his entire corn crop; with unshaken faith he wrote to God, sure that God sees everything and would not let his family go hungry. (b) The postmaster read the letter, laughed at first, then resolved to keep that faith alive; he gathered seventy pesos from employees and his own salary and sent it signed God. (c) After counting only seventy pesos, Lencho, sure God could not err, wrote asking for thirty more, adding that God should not send it through the mail because the post office employees were a bunch of crooks. The irony is sharp: the men he called crooks were his benefactors.

chapters.title: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom
chapters.summary: This extract from Nelson Mandela's autobiography, Long Walk to Freedom, describes his inauguration as the first democratically elected President of South Africa on 10 May 1994. Mandela honours the freedom fighters of the anti-apartheid struggle and reflects on courage, love and the true meaning of freedom. He concludes that freedom is indivisible and belongs to both the oppressed and the oppressor.
hotTopics: Inauguration ceremony of 10 May 1994
Apartheid and its effects on people
Twin obligations to family and country
Courage is not the absence of fear
Freedom for the oppressed and the oppressor
Two national anthems and the military salute

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: On 10 May 1994 the ceremonies took place in the lovely sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria, for decades the seat of white supremacy, now the site of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government.
Mr de Klerk was sworn in as the second deputy president and Thabo Mbeki as the first deputy president before Nelson Mandela took the oath as the first democratically elected President.
Military generals who would have arrested Mandela not many years earlier saluted him and pledged their loyalty, while the chevron of Impala jets trailed smoke in the colours of the new national flag.
Two national anthems were sung, Nkosi Sikelel iAfrika and Die Stem, and Mandela vowed that never, never again would this beautiful land experience the oppression of one by another.

Mandela recalled African patriots such as Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Chief Luthuli, Yusuf Dadoo, Bram Fischer and Robert Sobukwe, calling himself the sum of all those sacrifices, and named the people as the country's greatest wealth.

He reflected that no one is born hating another person, that courage is not the absence of fear, that every man has twin obligations, and that freedom is indivisible, owed to the oppressed and the oppressor alike.

keyTerms.meaning: the date of Mandela's inauguration as President
the venue of the inauguration ceremonies
the leader sworn in as second deputy president
the leader sworn in as first deputy president
Nkosi Sikelel iAfrika and Die Stem, sung together on the day
the planes that trailed the new flag's colours over the ceremony

sections.trick: Order of oaths: de Klerk (second), Mbeki (first), Mandela (President) - D-M-M; plus the date 10 May 1994.
sections.examPointer: Factual details of the ceremony (venue, deputies, jets, anthems) feed one-mark and extract questions; learn them as a single picture.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: Courage and sacrifice: the liberation of South Africa was won by patriots whose bravery Mandela honours on inauguration day.
Reconciliation: Mandela's forgiveness replaces revenge; even the generals of the old regime salute and pledge loyalty.
Twin obligations: every person owes duties to family and to community and country, and a just society allows both to be honoured.
Freedom is indivisible: chains on any one of the people are chains on all, and the oppressor too is a prisoner of hatred and prejudice.
Love over hate: people learn to hate and can be taught to love, for love comes more naturally to the human heart.
Message: true freedom means living with respect for the freedom of others, and courage means conquering fear, not avoiding it.

keyTerms.meaning: institutionalised racial discrimination that ruled South Africa earlier
the triumph over fear, not the absence of it
indivisible; it belongs to the oppressed and the oppressor alike
Mandela's forgiveness replacing the desire for revenge
love comes more naturally to the human heart than hate
Mandela's debt to the freedom fighters who sacrificed their lives

sections.trick: Theme formula: C-T-F-L - Courage, Twin obligations, Freedom indivisible, Love over hate; one sentence on each completes any LA.
sections.examPointer: The lines on hate and love, and on courage and fear, are the surest extract sources; memorise their exact meaning, not just the gist.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: Nelson Mandela is courageous and humble; he treats the inauguration not as a personal victory but as the triumph of justice, peace and human dignity.
Mandela is deeply grateful: he remembers patriots like Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu who could not see the day, calling himself the sum of their sacrifices.
Mandela is a reflective thinker: his insights on courage, hatred, obligations and freedom give the chapter its philosophical depth.
Mr de Klerk appears as the outgoing order's leader, sworn in as second deputy president, symbolising the transition of power.
Thabo Mbeki is sworn in as first deputy president, standing beside Mandela in the new government.
The people of South Africa are Mandela's heroes: he calls them the country's greatest wealth, finer than the most brilliant diamonds.

keyTerms.meaning: first democratically elected President of South Africa; humble, brave, visionary
sworn in as second deputy president at the ceremony
sworn in as first deputy president
patriots like Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu whom Mandela recalls
once Mandela's probable arresters, now saluting and pledging loyalty

sections.trick: Mandela's three roles: Statesman (inauguration), Grateful son (patriots), Philosopher (courage and freedom) - build the sketch on these three pillars.
sections.examPointer: For the character sketch LA, blend his humility, gratitude and wisdom with one ceremony detail and one philosophical quote.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: This chapter's vocabulary is political and ceremonial; revise both the word and the context in which it appears.
Apartheid-related words appear in value-based answers, so use them correctly while describing South Africa's past.
Ceremonial words like inauguration and amphitheatre describe the opening scene; pair them with the venue.
Transitory is used for the freedoms of youth; contrast it with the basic honourable freedoms.
Practise using chevron, oppressor and emancipation in sentences to fix their meanings.

keyTerms.meaning: a system of racial segregation and discrimination against non-whites in South Africa
the formal ceremony of installing a person in office
an open oval space formed by rising rows of seats
a V-shaped formation, used for the flying jets
lasting only for a short time, like the freedoms of youth
one who keeps others down by unjust use of power

sections.trick: Pair the words: inauguration-amphitheatre (ceremony), apartheid-oppressor (oppression), transitory-chevron (chapter-specific).
sections.examPointer: Definitions must carry context; 'apartheid' should be explained as racial segregation in South Africa, not merely 'discrimination'.

sections.heading: Exam Focus
points: Value-based angle: freedom is indivisible; no one is truly free while oppressing others - the surest value question from this chapter.
Extract-based passages usually come from the no one is born hating paragraph or the courage-is-not-the-absence-of-fear paragraph.
Facts to memorise: 10 May 1994, Union Buildings, Pretoria, de Klerk second deputy, Mbeki first deputy, two anthems, generals' salute.
Common SA questions: the twin obligations, why the oppressor is not free, what Mandela learned about courage and love.
For the LA, connect the ceremony (justice, peace, human dignity) with the sacrifices of the freedom fighters and the end of apartheid.

keyTerms.meaning: duty to one's family and duty to one's community and country
questions quoting the hate-love or courage-fear lines
answers on freedom, forgiveness and responsibility
the date examiners expect in every factual answer
Mandela's image of people of many colours and nations united

sections.trick: Say the date in every answer about this chapter: 10 May 1994 instantly anchors SA and LA responses in fact.
sections.examPointer: When asked what Mandela learned about freedom, move from boyhood freedom (illusion) to transitory freedoms to basic honourable freedoms - this ladder scores full marks.

mcqs.question: When was Nelson Mandela sworn in as the President of South Africa?
mcqs.explanation: The inauguration ceremonies took place on 10 May 1994.

mcqs.question: Where were the inauguration ceremonies held?
options: The amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria
mcqs.explanation: The lovely sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria hosted the ceremonies.

mcqs.question: Who was sworn in as the second deputy president?
mcqs.explanation: Mr de Klerk was sworn in as the second deputy president; Thabo Mbeki became the first deputy president.

mcqs.question: According to Mandela, what is a country's greatest wealth?
mcqs.explanation: Mandela says his country is rich in minerals and gems, but its greatest wealth is its people, finer than the most brilliant diamonds.

mcqs.question: "No one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion." What does Mandela conclude from this thought?
options: Hatred is permanent and must be feared
People learn to hate and can be taught to love, since love comes more naturally to the human heart
mcqs.explanation: Mandela argues that hatred is learnt; if people can learn to hate, they can be taught to love, for love is more natural to the heart.

mcqs.question: What did the jets do during the inauguration ceremony?
options: Flew over the Union Buildings trailing smoke in the colours of the new flag
mcqs.explanation: The chevron of Impala jets roared over the Union Buildings trailing smoke in the colours of the new South African flag.

mcqs.question: What are the 'twin obligations' every man has, according to Mandela?
options: To his family and to his community and country
To his past and to his future
To his religion and to his nation
mcqs.explanation: Mandela says a man has obligations to his family, parents, wife and children, and also to his community and country.

mcqs.question: Which two national anthems were sung on inauguration day?
options: God Save the Queen and Die Stem
Nkosi Sikelel iAfrika and Die Stem
Die Stem and a new anthem
mcqs.explanation: Both the anthem of the blacks, Nkosi Sikelel iAfrika, and the old anthem of the whites, Die Stem, were sung, symbolising unity.

mcqs.question: "The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear." What is Mandela's idea of courage here?
options: Courage means the absence of fear
Courage is the triumph over fear
Courage is a gift of birth
mcqs.explanation: Mandela learned that courage is not the absence of fear but the victory over it; everyone feels afraid, the brave act anyway.

mcqs.question: Why does Mandela say that the oppressor is also not free?
options: He lives in constant fear of the courts
He is a prisoner of hatred, locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness
He is bound by his army
mcqs.explanation: Mandela believes both the oppressed and the oppressor are robbed of their humanity; the oppressor is imprisoned by hatred and prejudice.

boardQuestions.question: What did the military generals do at the inauguration, and why is it significant?
boardQuestions.answer: The highest generals of the South African defence force and police, who would have arrested Mandela not many years before, saluted him and pledged their loyalty. The salute of the very men who guarded apartheid showed that the old racial order had accepted the new non-racial democracy.

boardQuestions.question: What are the 'twin obligations' according to Nelson Mandela?
boardQuestions.answer: According to Mandela, every man has twin obligations: one to his family, to his parents, wife and children, and the other to his community and his country. In a free and just society a person can honour both together, but under oppression a man is unable to fulfil either properly.

boardQuestions.question: How did Mandela describe the country's greatest wealth and the patriots on inauguration day?
boardQuestions.answer: Mandela said his country was rich in minerals and gems, but its greatest wealth was its people, finer than the purest diamonds. On inauguration day he recalled African patriots such as Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Chief Luthuli, Yusuf Dadoo, Bram Fischer and Robert Sobukwe, who had paid with their lives and could not be present, and he described himself as the sum of all those sacrifices.

boardQuestions.question: How did Mandela's idea of freedom change from boyhood to his youth in Johannesburg?
boardQuestions.answer: As a boy Mandela was born free: he could run in the fields and swim in the stream, though he later realised this boyhood freedom was an illusion. As a student he craved transitory freedoms, like staying out at night or going where he chose. In Johannesburg he yearned for the basic honourable freedoms of achieving his potential, earning his keep, marrying and having a family, and when these were denied he understood that freedom is indivisible.

boardQuestions.question: 'No one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion.' How does Mandela's reflection on love and hate guide society towards harmony?
boardQuestions.answer: Mandela begins from the truth that hatred is not natural but learnt; nobody is born hating another person for his skin colour, background or religion. Since hate is taught, it can also be untaught: if people can learn to hate, they can be taught to love, because love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite. This insight let Mandela free his own heart from bitterness instead of seeking revenge, as his reconciliation with the very generals who once jailed him shows. For society the message is clear: families, schools and leaders must consciously teach tolerance, and individuals must guard their minds against the poison of discrimination, so that harmony replaces conflict.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the inauguration ceremony of 10 May 1994 and explain why Mandela calls it a triumph of justice, peace and human dignity.
boardQuestions.answer: On 10 May 1994 the ceremonies took place in the sandstone amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, once the seat of white supremacy. Mr de Klerk was sworn in as the second deputy president, Thabo Mbeki as the first, and Nelson Mandela as the first democratically elected President of South Africa. Military generals who could have arrested him earlier saluted him, Impala jets trailed the colours of the new flag, and two national anthems, Nkosi Sikelel iAfrika and Die Stem, were sung. Mandela vowed never again would the land see the oppression of one by another. He calls it a triumph not of any party or man but of justice, peace and human dignity, because apartheid's racial order was replaced by a rainbow gathering of equals.

boardQuestions.question: "Courage is not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it. The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear." Answer the questions that follow: (a) What, according to Mandela, is real courage? (b) How did he learn this truth? (c) How can this idea help a student facing examination fear?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) Mandela learned that courage is not the absence of fear; the brave are those who feel afraid yet conquer that fear by acting despite it. (b) He says he learned this through the times and experiences of the freedom struggle, watching comrades endure threats, prison and sacrifice without abandoning the cause. (c) For a student, the idea means accepting nervousness before an examination as natural and going ahead with preparation and confidence; fear is overcome by facing it, just as the brave act despite fear. Thus anxiety, when confronted, turns into courage.

chapters.title: Two Stories about Flying
chapters.summary: This chapter pairs two flying stories. In His First Flight by Liam O'Flaherty, a young seagull crippled by fear is pushed by hunger and its mother's clever bait into making its first flight. In The Black Aeroplane by Frederick Forsyth, a pilot lost in a storm with dead instruments is guided to safety by a mysterious black aeroplane that never appears on the radar.
hotTopics: The young seagull's fear of flying
Hunger as the driving force
The mother seagull's trick with the fish
The mysterious black aeroplane
Compass and radio failing in the storm
Value angle: courage overcomes fear

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: A young seagull was alone on its ledge while its two brothers and sister had flown away the day before; though his wings were as strong as theirs, he felt certain they would never support him.
The whole family had taunted him with cowardice and his parents threatened to let him starve on the ledge; the sun blazed higher and his hunger grew, while he pretended to sleep on one leg.
Seeing his mother with a piece of fish, the famished seagull begged for food; when she halted just out of reach of his beak, he dived at the fish, lost his footing and fell into space.

A monstrous terror seized him and his heart stood still, but instinct flapped his wings; he soared over the green sea, landed safely, ate the fish, and his family circled him offering scraps of dog-fish.

In The Black Aeroplane, the narrator flies his old Dakota DS 088 from Paris to England at one-thirty in the morning, dreaming of a holiday and a big English breakfast, while Paris control directs him twelve degrees west.

Inside huge storm clouds the compass, radio and other instruments go dead; a strange black aeroplane appears and its waving pilot leads him southwards to a safe landing with only five or ten minutes of fuel left, though the control room says no other aeroplane was seen on radar that night.

keyTerms.meaning: the rock shelf where the young seagull sat alone
the bait that lured the seagull into flight
the fear that froze the seagull as he fell
the water on which the flying family landed
the old plane the narrator flew towards England
the control room's puzzling reply about the black plane

sections.trick: Split the chapter in your head: Story 1 = fear beaten by hunger; Story 2 = crisis beaten by a mystery. Never mix the details of the two.
sections.examPointer: Examiners set separate questions on each story; tag every fact you quote with the correct story to avoid losing marks.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: Fear is often imaginary: the seagull's wings were as strong as his siblings', yet doubt kept him on the ledge.
Necessity is the strongest motivator: hunger finally pushed the seagull to act where threats had failed.
Tough love: the mother's deliberate halt out of reach shows that encouragement sometimes needs a strategic push.
Courage in crisis: the pilot of the Dakota keeps calm, follows the strange plane and lands safely with almost no fuel.
The unknown need not be hostile: the mysterious black aeroplane suggests unseen help or providence for those in desperate need.
Message: face your fears with action and keep hope in adversity; confidence comes from attempting, never from hesitating.

keyTerms.meaning: the imaginary barrier that prevents the first attempt
acting despite fear, as both seagull and pilot must
the necessity that drives the seagull to dive
the mother's deliberate test with the fish
the unexplained black aeroplane and its pilot
unseen help that rescues the desperate pilot

sections.trick: Theme pair: F-H-C-M - Fear, Hunger, Courage, Mystery; quote one example for each and the LA is complete.
sections.examPointer: Compare-and-contrast questions are common: the seagull conquers fear by himself, the pilot is saved by outside help; bring out this difference.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: The young seagull is timid, hesitant and full of self-doubt despite having strong wings; he even plays the trick of standing on one leg and pretending to sleep.
Once airborne, the same seagull becomes joyful and confident, curving, banking and diving around his family - showing fear was his only enemy.
The mother seagull is loving but wise: she knows food alone will not work, so she uses the fish as bait and halts just out of reach.
The father seagull and the rest of the family are strict yet caring; they taunt the cowardice, but fly around the young one and feed him after his success.
The pilot of the Dakota is skilled and calm in crisis; he follows the stranger's guidance and honestly admits he cannot explain the rescue.
The black aeroplane's pilot is a silent, unidentified helper - a symbol of providence or of unknown human kindness.

keyTerms.meaning: timid and self-doubting, but capable once he acts
wise and loving; uses hunger and bait strategically
strict parent who taunts the young one's cowardice
two brothers and a sister already flying confidently
calm, grateful and honest about the mystery
silent rescuer who is never identified

sections.trick: Sketch with contrast: the same bird is coward and hero within one scene - his only change is action; that is the sketch's pivot.
sections.examPointer: If asked to sketch the mother seagull, stress her understanding of psychology: threats failed, hunger worked - support with the fish episode.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: The chapter mixes bird-story words (ledge, brink, plateau) with flying words (Dakota, compass, radar); learn them in these two groups.
Vocabulary questions often come as fill-in-the-blank from the text, so pair every word with its exact context.
Explain technical words like radar simply: a device that shows aircraft on screens.
Note phrases like scraps of dog-fish and a monstrous terror; they appear in extracts.
Revise spellings of ledge, brink and plateau together to avoid confusion.

keyTerms.meaning: a narrow rocky shelf on the cliff where the seagull sat
the very edge of the ledge
an area of flat high ground where the family walked
an old type of transport aeroplane flown by the narrator
the instrument showing direction; it failed in the storm
the electronic screen system that detected no other plane

sections.trick: Bird group: L-B-P (ledge, brink, plateau); Plane group: D-C-R (Dakota, compass, radar) - six words, two rows.
sections.examPointer: When extracts quote the storm or the ledge, use these exact words in your answers to show textual accuracy.

sections.heading: Exam Focus
points: Value-based angle: overcoming fear builds confidence (seagull); faith and presence of mind in crisis (pilot) - both fit value questions.
Contrast questions are common: why threats failed and hunger worked; how the seagull's first dive changed him forever.
Extract-based passages usually quote the mother halting with the fish, the monstrous terror lines, or the nothing-on-radar reply.
Learn the exact details: two brothers and a sister, the piece of fish, the green sea, scraps of dog-fish, DS 088, twelve degrees west, five or ten minutes of fuel.
For long answers, compare the two stories: fear conquered by action (seagull) versus help beyond explanation (pilot), and end with the common message of courage.

keyTerms.meaning: quoted passages from the fish episode or the storm
answers on overcoming fear and facing crisis
comparing the two stories' heroes and outcomes
siblings, fish, DS 088, 12 degrees west, 5-10 minutes fuel
the deliberate suspense of the black aeroplane's identity

sections.trick: Number bank: 2 brothers + 1 sister; DS 088; 12 degrees west; 5-10 minutes fuel - examiners love these exact figures.
sections.examPointer: Never call the black aeroplane a ghost in answers; write 'mysterious' or 'unexplained', and add that the pilot could not identify his rescuer.

mcqs.question: Who were already flying when the young seagull was alone on the ledge?
options: His two brothers and his sister
Nobody - he was the first to fly
mcqs.explanation: The young seagull's two brothers and sister had already flown away the day before.

mcqs.question: What tempted the young seagull to make his first flight?
options: A piece of fish held by his mother
A loud call from his father
mcqs.explanation: Maddened by hunger at the sight of the fish his mother carried, the seagull dived at it and slipped off the ledge.

mcqs.question: What type of aeroplane was the narrator flying in The Black Aeroplane?
mcqs.explanation: The narrator was flying his old Dakota aeroplane, DS 088, from Paris to England.

mcqs.question: What reply did the woman in the control room give about the black aeroplane?
options: It belonged to the air force
No other aeroplane was seen on the radar that night
It had crashed into the sea
mcqs.explanation: The woman replied that no other aeroplane was seen on the radar that night, deepening the mystery.

mcqs.question: "His mother had halted in the air, keeping herself just out of reach of his beak." Why did the mother seagull halt at that distance?
options: She wanted to punish the young bird
She wanted the young bird to dive and fly to get the fish
She was afraid of falling herself
She wanted to teach him to swim
mcqs.explanation: Knowing that only hunger could overcome his fear, she used the fish as bait to force him into his first flight.

mcqs.question: What happened to the young seagull as he fell from the ledge?
options: His heart beat faster with joy
A monstrous terror seized him and his heart stood still
mcqs.explanation: A monstrous terror seized him and his heart stood still as he fell into space, before instinct made his wings work.

mcqs.question: Which instruments of the narrator's plane stopped working inside the storm clouds?
options: The compass, the radio and the other instruments
mcqs.explanation: Inside the black clouds the plane jumped and twisted; the compass, the radio and the other instruments stopped working.

mcqs.question: Why did the narrator follow the strange black aeroplane?
options: He had no working compass or radio and was almost out of fuel
He wanted to race the plane
The airport ordered him to follow
mcqs.explanation: Lost in the storm with dead instruments and fuel for only five or ten minutes, he gratefully followed the black aeroplane to safety.

mcqs.question: "Inside the clouds, everything was suddenly black. The old aeroplane jumped and twisted in the air." What does this description emphasise about the narrator's situation?
options: A life-threatening crisis in which he was lost and helpless
The pleasure of flying at night
mcqs.explanation: The darkness, the jumping plane and the dead instruments show the pilot facing mortal danger, blind and directionless.

mcqs.question: Which detail best makes the black aeroplane 'mysterious'?
options: It flew faster than the Dakota
It had no lights and never appeared on the radar records though it guided the narrator to safety
mcqs.explanation: The strange plane appeared in a storm, guided the narrator out, and then the control room confirmed nothing was on the radar - an unexplained mystery.

boardQuestions.question: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly even though his wings were strong?
boardQuestions.answer: The young seagull felt certain that his great wings would never support him, so he dared not flap them. He feared the long fall to the sea far below the ledge, and when he ran to the brink he became afraid and returned to his little hole under the ledge where he slept at night.

boardQuestions.question: What difficulties did the pilot of the Dakota face inside the storm clouds?
boardQuestions.answer: Inside the huge black clouds everything turned dark and the old aeroplane jumped and twisted in the air. The compass, the radio and all the other instruments stopped working, and the pilot could not contact Paris control. With fuel enough for only five or ten minutes, he was lost and completely helpless.

boardQuestions.question: How did the mother seagull succeed in making the young seagull fly where threats had failed?
boardQuestions.answer: The parents had called to him shrilly, upbraided him for his cowardice and threatened to let him starve on his ledge, but fear kept him grounded. The mother then flew to him carrying a piece of fish and, when the hungry bird dived at it, she halted just out of reach of his beak. Maddened by hunger, the seagull plunged at the fish, fell off the ledge and, flapping his wings in terror, discovered that he could fly.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the mystery of the black aeroplane and the landing at the airport.
boardQuestions.answer: When the Dakota's instruments failed inside the storm, a strange black aeroplane appeared beside the narrator. Its pilot waved and turned his plane slowly to the south; the narrator, with fuel for only five or ten minutes, followed gratefully and landed safely. When he looked back for the black aeroplane, it was gone, and the woman in the control centre said no other aeroplane had been seen on the radar that night.

boardQuestions.question: 'Fear is the greatest obstacle to success; courage overcomes it.' Discuss with reference to His First Flight.
boardQuestions.answer: The young seagull possessed wings as strong as his siblings', yet believed they would never carry him; his fear, not his ability, chained him to the ledge. The family's taunts and threats failed, but hunger and the mother's clever bait did what encouragement could not: when he dived at the fish, terror made his heart stand still, yet instinct flapped his wings and he soared over the green sea. Soon he was curving, banking, diving and screaming with joy, completely forgetting he had ever been afraid. The story teaches that fear grows in inaction and dies in action; the first step, however frightening, reveals abilities we doubted we had.

boardQuestions.question: Narrate the experience of the pilot in The Black Aeroplane. Why does the story remain a mystery?
boardQuestions.answer: Flying his old Dakota from Paris to England at one-thirty in the morning, the pilot dreams of a holiday and a big English breakfast while Paris control tells him to turn twelve degrees west. A hundred and fifty kilometres from England he enters huge storm clouds; the plane jumps and twists, the compass and radio die, and he is lost with fuel for five or ten minutes. Suddenly a strange black aeroplane appears; its pilot waves and leads him southwards out of the storm to a safe landing. When the control room says no other aeroplane was seen on radar that night, and the black aeroplane is gone from the sky, the rescuer remains unexplained. The mystery suggests unseen help or providence guiding those in desperate need.

boardQuestions.question: "The mother flew over to him with a piece of fish, but when she was just opposite to him she halted, keeping herself just out of reach of his beak." Answer the questions that follow: (a) Why had the young seagull not flown so far? (b) Why did the mother halt out of reach, and what did the seagull do next? (c) What lesson does this episode teach?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) The young seagull, though his wings were as strong as his siblings', was convinced they would not support him, so he stayed on the ledge while the whole family flew. (b) The mother carried a piece of fish and halted just out of his beak's reach; maddened by hunger, he dived at the fish, fell off the ledge and, flapping his wings, began to fly. (c) The episode teaches that love must sometimes test us rather than pamper us, and that fear is conquered only by taking the plunge - action converts fear into confidence.

chapters.title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
chapters.summary: This chapter presents extracts from the diary that Anne Frank began on her thirteenth birthday, 12 June 1942, and addressed to an imaginary friend named Kitty. Anne writes about why she confides in paper, her family, the anti-Jewish laws and her amusing battle with the maths teacher Mr Keesing. Her last entry records the call-up notice that forced the family into hiding in July 1942.
hotTopics: Kitty, the diary as an imaginary friend
Paper has more patience than people
Mr Keesing's essays and the duck poem
Anti-Jewish restrictions after May 1940
Anne's family background and loneliness
The entry of 8 July 1942 and hiding

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: Anne Frank, born on 12 June 1929 in Frankfurt, began her diary on her thirteenth birthday in June 1942 and wrote to it as Kitty, an imaginary friend to whom she could confide everything.

Calling writing in a diary a strange experience for a thirteen-year-old schoolgirl, she still resolved to write, since paper has more patience than people and nobody seemed likely to be interested in a schoolgirl's feelings.

Her father emigrated to Holland in 1933 when Hitler came to power; her parents had married in 1925, Margot was born in Frankfurt in 1926 and Anne in 1929, and her beloved grandmother died in January 1942.

After the German occupation of May 1940, anti-Jewish laws followed: wearing the yellow star, surrendering bicycles, bans on trams and driving, shopping only between three and five in Jewish shops, evening curfews, and attendance at Jewish schools only.

Talkative Anne annoyed her maths teacher, Mr Keesing, who punished her with extra essays; after A Chatterbox and An Incorrigible Chatterbox, she turned Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Quackenbush into a poem with her friend Sanne's help, and Mr Keesing, taking the joke well, stopped assigning extra homework.

In her entry of 8 July 1942, Anne records the call-up notice from the SS and the family's hurried move into hiding the next morning, walking through the rain with schoolbags and shopping bags and leaving her cat Moortje with the neighbours.

keyTerms.meaning: the name Anne gives her diary, her imaginary friend
Anne's thirteenth birthday, when the diary began
the maths teacher who punished talkative Anne
the first essay Anne wrote as punishment

keyTerms.term: Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Quackenbush
keyTerms.meaning: the third topic, which Anne turned into a poem
the SS summons that pushed the family into hiding

sections.trick: Essay ladder: Chatterbox, Incorrigible, Quack-Quack - three strikes and Keesing joined Anne's side; dates to hold: 1942 diary, 1933 Holland move.
sections.examPointer: Any answer on Anne should open with Kitty and the June 1942 start; extract questions come most often from the paper-and-patience and Keesing passages.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: Loneliness of adolescence: Anne needs a confidant she cannot find, so she invents Kitty and treats the diary as a real friend.
The healing power of writing: paper has more patience than people, and pouring out her heart keeps Anne balanced.
Suffering under discrimination: the anti-Jewish laws show how a hateful system crushes the ordinary life of a schoolgirl.
Wit and courage in adversity: Anne turns punishment into victory through humour and intelligence.
Family love and loss: warm sketches of her parents and Margot, and deep grief for her grandmother who died in January 1942.
Message: self-expression builds resilience; hope, humour and honesty can survive even persecution.

keyTerms.meaning: Anne's need for a confidant like Kitty
paper's patience heals and preserves her thoughts
the anti-Jewish laws that crush normal life
humour defeats punishment, as in the Keesing essays
Anne's warmth towards her parents, Margot and grandmother
hope and humour surviving persecution

sections.trick: Theme set L-W-D-W-F: Loneliness, Writing, Discrimination, Wit, Family - five threads that knit every answer on this chapter.
sections.examPointer: Value questions ask why Anne writes to Kitty; answer with the patience-of-paper idea plus the loneliness of a thirteen-year-old under oppression.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: Anne Frank is lively, talkative, intelligent and self-aware; she describes classmates and teachers with sharp humour.
She is sensitive and lonely: she wants a true friend in whom to confide everything, so she addresses the diary as Kitty.
She is witty and bold: in A Chatterbox she argues that talking is an inherited female trait, and her duck poem finally wins over Mr Keesing.
Mr Keesing is the old fogey maths teacher: strict and annoyed by Anne's chatter, yet broad-minded enough to laugh, read her poem aloud and end the punishment.
Margot is Anne's elder sister, born in Frankfurt in 1926, and Sanne is the friend who helps Anne turn the third essay into verse.
Anne's father, Otto Frank, is remembered as the most adorable father she has ever seen, and her grandmother, who died in January 1942, remains dear to her.

keyTerms.meaning: talkative, intelligent, witty and self-aware thirteen-year-old diarist
strict maths teacher, fair and humour-loving at heart
Anne's elder sister, born in Frankfurt in 1926
Anne's friend who helped her write the duck poem
Anne's father, the most adorable father she has ever seen
the beloved relative who died in January 1942

sections.trick: Pair the sketch: Anne (chatter, wit, courage) vs Keesing (strictness, fairness) - their duel and reconciliation is the heart of the chapter.
sections.examPointer: Character questions reward balance: show Anne's faults (talkativeness) along with her virtues (wit, honesty), and Keesing's strictness with his fairness.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: The chapter's key words describe Anne's inner life and the punishment episode; learn them with the diary context.
Unbosomings and confide belong to the writing theme; chatterbox and incorrigible belong to the Keesing theme.
Call-up notice is a historical term; explain it as an official order to report for duty.
Use each word in a line about Anne to fix its meaning and spelling together.
These words often appear as match-the-meaning or one-mark items, so revise them before every test.

keyTerms.meaning: to share private thoughts and secrets with someone trusted
revelations of one's innermost feelings
a person who talks too much
too bad to be corrected or reformed
an official order to report for service
left one's country to settle in another

sections.trick: Writing pair: confide-unbosomings; Punishment pair: chatterbox-incorrigible; History pair: call-up-emigrated.
sections.examPointer: Define 'incorrigible' precisely (impossible to correct); vague meanings like 'bad' lose marks in word-meaning items.

sections.heading: Exam Focus
points: Value-based angle: writing as emotional strength; courage and humour under persecution - the diary as both friend and history.
Fact bank to memorise: Kitty; thirteenth birthday, 12 June 1942; father emigrated to Holland in 1933; Margot born 1926; grandmother died January 1942; the three essay titles; the 8 July 1942 entry.
Extract-based passages usually come from the paper-has-more-patience lines, the anti-Jewish laws list, or the Keesing poem outcome.
Short questions ask why Anne began a diary, why Keesing was annoyed, what happened to the third essay, and how the laws changed her life.
For long answers, contrast Anne and Keesing, or show how the diary reveals both a normal schoolgirl and a victim of history; end with the significance of the last entry.

keyTerms.meaning: hot quotes: patience lines, Keesing entries, the poem outcome
writing as strength; humour and courage in dark times
Kitty, 1942, 1933 Holland, three essay titles
first-person narration by a thirteen-year-old
the entry marking the end of normal life as hiding begins

sections.trick: Title ladder chant: Chatterbox - Incorrigible - Quack Quack Quack; recite it and the whole Keesing episode unfolds in order.
sections.examPointer: Always connect Anne's school-life fun with the darker frame (laws, hiding) in five-mark answers; examiners look for both worlds in one response.

mcqs.question: What name did Anne give to her diary?
mcqs.explanation: Anne addressed her diary as Kitty, treating it like an intimate friend.

mcqs.question: On what occasion did Anne begin writing her diary?
options: When her family went into hiding
mcqs.explanation: Anne received and began the diary on her thirteenth birthday, 12 June 1942.

mcqs.question: Which subject did Mr Keesing teach?
mcqs.explanation: Mr Keesing was the maths teacher whom Anne calls an old fogey.

mcqs.question: In which year did Anne's father emigrate to Holland?
mcqs.explanation: Anne records that her father emigrated to Holland in 1933, when Hitler came to power.

mcqs.question: "Paper has more patience than people." Why does Anne prefer confiding in her diary?
options: Because paper never interrupts or judges her
Because she dislikes her family and friends
Because she wants to become a published writer
Because her friends refuse to listen to her
mcqs.explanation: Unlike people, paper does not interrupt, argue or judge, so Anne can pour out her feelings freely to Kitty.

mcqs.question: What was the topic of the first essay Mr Keesing assigned as punishment?
mcqs.explanation: Because Anne talked so much in class, the old fogey first made her write an essay called A Chatterbox.

mcqs.question: Which of these restrictions on Jews does Anne mention?
options: They could not ride trams and had to hand in their bicycles
They were given free bicycles by the state
They could shop anywhere at any time
They were exempt from attending school
mcqs.explanation: Anne lists the yellow star, surrendering bicycles, the tram ban, curfew hours, restricted shopping hours and Jewish schools only.

mcqs.question: Who helped Anne convert the third essay topic into a poem in verse?
mcqs.explanation: Anne's friend Sanne, good at poetry, helped her write the duck-family verse for Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Quackenbush.

mcqs.question: "Writing in a diary is a really strange experience for someone like me. Not only because I've never written anything before, but also because it seems to me that later on neither I nor anyone else will be interested in the unbosomings of a thirteen-year-old schoolgirl." What does this entry reveal about Anne?
options: Her honesty, self-doubt and natural humour
Her hatred of school and teachers
Her plan to publish the diary
mcqs.explanation: Anne candidly doubts whether anyone would care for a schoolgirl's outpourings, yet she writes on - showing self-awareness, humour and honesty.

mcqs.question: What deeper significance does the entry dated 8 July 1942 carry in the chapter?
options: It marks the end of normal life as the family received a call-up notice and went into hiding
It lists the names of her friends
mcqs.explanation: The entry about the call-up notice and the hurried move into hiding shows persecution invading the schoolgirl's everyday world.

boardQuestions.question: Who was Kitty and why did Anne confide in her?
boardQuestions.answer: Kitty was the name Anne Frank gave to her diary, which she began on her thirteenth birthday in June 1942. Since she had no friend in whom she could confide everything, she treated the diary as an imaginary friend and wrote to it as if replying to her letters.

boardQuestions.question: Why did Mr Keesing punish Anne Frank?
boardQuestions.answer: Mr Keesing, the maths teacher, was annoyed because Anne talked too much in class. To check her chatterbox habit he gave her extra homework in the form of essays, the first being A Chatterbox, on the very subject of her talkativeness.

boardQuestions.question: How did Anne argue in her essay A Chatterbox, and with what result?
boardQuestions.answer: Anne wrote three arguments in the essay: talking is a female trait, her mother talked as much as she did, if not more, and little could be done about inherited traits. Mr Keesing had a good laugh at her arguments, though he soon set her a second essay, An Incorrigible Chatterbox, which showed he was still not fully satisfied.

boardQuestions.question: What changes came into the lives of the Jews after the German occupation of Holland, according to Anne?
boardQuestions.answer: After May 1940 the good times were few and anti-Jewish laws came one after another. Jews had to wear a yellow star and surrender their bicycles; they were banned from trams and forbidden to drive. They could shop only between three and five in Jewish shops, children could attend only Jewish schools, and they were forbidden to go out between eight in the evening and six in the morning.

boardQuestions.question: Sketch the character of Anne Frank as revealed in her diary entries.
boardQuestions.answer: Anne comes across as a lively, talkative thirteen-year-old, honest about her own faults and aware that few would read a schoolgirl's diary. Her confiding in Kitty shows her loneliness and her deep need for a true friend. She is witty and bold: facing Mr Keesing's repeated punishments, she argues cleverly that talking is an inherited female trait and then, with Sanne's help, turns the third topic into a poem about a quacking duck family, which makes even the stern teacher laugh. She is also sensitive and loving, sketching her adorable father, her mother and sister Margot, and mourning her grandmother who died in January 1942. Above all she is observant and resilient, recording the humiliating anti-Jewish laws with clear eyes and keeping humour alive in dark times.

boardQuestions.question: 'Paper has more patience than people.' Bring out the significance of this idea in Anne's life as a writer.
boardQuestions.answer: Anne feels that people are rarely interested in a thirteen-year-old's feelings; they interrupt, do not listen or react impatiently, while paper silently waits and lets her pour out whatever is on her heart. That is why she gives the diary a name, Kitty, and treats it as a friend who will never judge her. Writing becomes her way of thinking: she confides her loneliness, her family, her classmates and her battles with Mr Keesing, turning troubles into light, humorous prose. The idea also explains why the diary survives as literature - the patience of paper preserved the voice of a young girl facing persecution, proving that self-expression can be both therapy and history.

boardQuestions.question: "Mr Keesing took the joke the right way. He read the poem to the class, adding his own comments, and to several other classes as well. Since then I've been allowed to talk and haven't been assigned any extra homework." Answer the questions that follow: (a) Why had Mr Keesing been punishing Anne? (b) How did the poem change his attitude? (c) What does the episode reveal about Anne and Mr Keesing?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) Mr Keesing punished Anne with extra essays because she talked too much in his maths class, setting first A Chatterbox and then An Incorrigible Chatterbox. (b) For the third topic, Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Quackenbush, Anne, helped by her friend Sanne, wrote a poem in verse about a family of ducklings whose father-swan killed them for quacking too much; Mr Keesing took the joke the right way, read it aloud to the class and other classes too, and stopped assigning extra homework. (c) The episode reveals Anne's wit, courage and talent, and Mr Keesing's basic fairness and good humour beneath his strictness.

chapters.title: Glimpses of India
chapters.summary: Three travel sketches present India's variety. Lucio Rodrigues recalls the pader, the traditional bread-seller of Goa, whose kabai and bol still live in Goan memory. Lokesh Abrol paints Coorg as a land of rainforests, coffee and brave, hospitable people, while Arup Kumar Dutta follows two schoolboys to the tea gardens of Assam, full of facts and legends about over eighty crore cups of tea drunk daily.
hotTopics: The pader and the kabai of Goa
Bol, bolinhas and Goan festivals
Coorg: rainforests, coffee and the Kaveri
General Cariappa and Coorgi valour
Legends of the origin of tea
Tea gardens of Assam and the second flush

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: In A Baker from Goa, the narrator recalls his elders' nostalgia for the Portuguese days and their famous loaves of bread; the makers still exist and the fire in their furnaces has not yet been extinguished.

The pader made a musical entry with the jhang, jhang of his bamboo staff, basket on his head; children flocked for bread bangles, marriage gifts were meaningless without the sweet bol, and cakes and bolinhas were a must for Christmas and other festivals.

The baker wore the kabai, a single-piece long frock reaching the knees, collected bills at the end of the month, and, since baking was profitable, he and his family always looked plump and prosperous.

In Coorg, Lokesh Abrol describes Kodagu, the smallest district of Karnataka, midway between Mysore and Mangalore, home to evergreen rainforests, spices and coffee, best visited from September to March; the river Kaveri takes its water from Coorg's lake and woods, with mahaseer fish in its waters.

The Coorgis are brave and hospitable: their regiment is among the most decorated, General Cariappa was the first Chief of the Indian Army, the Kodavus may carry firearms without a licence, their origin is traced to Greek or Arab descent (the kuppia resembling the kuffia), and visitors enjoy Nisargadhama, the Brahmagiri hills and the monks of Bylakuppe.

In Tea from Assam, Rajvir and Pranjol travel to Assam; Rajvir shares that over eighty crore cups of tea are drunk daily and chai and chini are Chinese words, recalls the legends of the emperor and Bodhidharma, and at the Dhekiabari Tea Estate, managed by Pranjol's father, the boys see pluckers with bamboo baskets gathering the second flush, the sprouting period of May to July that yields the best tea.

keyTerms.meaning: Portuguese word for the baker of Goa
the baker's one-piece long frock to the knees
the sweet bread without which marriage gifts were meaningless
Coorg, the smallest district of Karnataka
the river fed by Coorg's lake and woods
the May-July sprouting season giving the best tea

sections.trick: Author-to-region map: Rodrigues-Roti (Goa), Abrol-Aroma (Coorg), Dutta-Chai (Assam); attach one signature detail to each (kabai, Kaveri, second flush).
sections.examPointer: Questions are set separately on each part; name the part and the author in every answer to show you know the three-piece structure.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: Unity in diversity: three regions, three livelihoods, one rich cultural heritage of India.
Living tradition: the paders still bake and the furnace fire still burns, showing that old professions survive change.
Nature's bounty: Coorg's coffee and rainforests and Assam's tea gardens show how land shapes livelihood and temperament.
Valour and hospitality: Coorgi pride in soldiers like General Cariappa goes hand in hand with warmth towards guests.
Curiosity as learning: Rajvir's excitement and reading versus Pranjol's boredom shows that interest turns travel into knowledge.
Message: cherish regional heritage - bread, coffee and tea are not mere products but living culture and history.

keyTerms.meaning: three regions, one Indian heritage
the paders still bake; the furnace fire burns on
coffee, spices and tea shaping regional life
the Coorgi pride in their decorated regiment
Rajvir's zest versus Pranjol's indifference
everyday foods carrying history and legend

sections.trick: Three S's of the chapter: Snack (Goa), Scenery (Coorg), Sip (Assam) - one theme sentence each and diversity is proved.
sections.examPointer: Value questions often ask how the chapter celebrates India's diversity; answer with one concrete example from each of the three parts.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: The Goan baker (pader) is a musical, friendly figure - the household's daily companion, plump and prosperous, a symbol of a living tradition.
The narrator of A Baker from Goa is a nostalgic Goan writer recording childhood memories and folk pride in the Portuguese-era bread.
The Coorgi people are fiercely brave and warmly hospitable: their regiment is one of the most decorated, and General Cariappa, the first Chief of the Indian Army, was a Coorgi.
Rajvir is a curious, well-read and observant Delhi schoolboy, fascinated by the tea gardens and eager to share legends and facts.
Pranjol, born and brought up among the tea gardens, buries himself in a detective book and shows little wonder - familiarity dulls his curiosity.
Pranjol's father is the manager of the Dhekiabari Tea Estate, a practical tea man who receives the boys at the garden.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: The chapter's vocabulary is regional and technical; group it as Goan words (pader, kabai, bol, bolinhas), Coorg words (mahaseer, kuppia) and tea words (second flush, plucker).
Explain Portuguese-origin words with their local use rather than literal translation.
Pair kuppia with kuffia since the comparison supports the Arab-origin theory and appears in extracts.
Use each term in a sentence describing its region to fix spelling and sense together.
These words recur in extract-based and one-mark items, so revise them part-wise.

sections.trick: Say the pairs aloud: kabai-bol (Goa), mahaseer-kuppia (Coorg), flush-plucker (Assam) - three regions, six words.
sections.examPointer: In answers about the baker's dress, write 'kabai, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees'; the definition inside the sentence earns full credit.

sections.heading: Exam Focus
points: Value-based angle: respect for traditional occupations (the pader), pride in diversity (Coorg), and curiosity as a tool of learning (Rajvir).

Fact bank: Lucio Rodrigues, Lokesh Abrol, Arup Kumar Dutta as writers; kabai and bol; smallest district of Karnataka; Kaveri; General Cariappa; firearms without licence; kuppia-kuffia; eighty crore cups; second flush May-July; Bodhidharma.
Extract-based passages usually quote the baker's entry and dress, the Kaveri-mahaseer description, or the tea legends including Bodhidharma's eyelids.
Short questions ask why bread is essential in Goa, the Coorgis' brave people and origin theories, why Pranjol was unexcited, and the three legends of tea.
For long answers, describe one region in your own words, compare Rajvir and Pranjol, or trace tea's journey from legend to everyday drink.

mcqs.question: Who wrote A Baker from Goa?
mcqs.explanation: A Baker from Goa is a nostalgic piece by Lucio Rodrigues about the Goan pader.

mcqs.question: What was the traditional dress of the Goan baker called?
mcqs.explanation: The bakers wore the kabai, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees.

mcqs.question: Coorg, or Kodagu, is the smallest district of which state?
mcqs.explanation: Lokesh Abrol calls Coorg the smallest district of Karnataka, midway between Mysore and Mangalore.

mcqs.question: Which large freshwater fish is mentioned as being found in Coorg's waters?
mcqs.explanation: The mahaseer, a large freshwater fish, abounds in the waters fed by the Kaveri.

mcqs.question: According to the text, how much tea is drunk every day throughout the world?
mcqs.explanation: Rajvir quotes the fact that over eighty crore cups of tea are drunk daily worldwide.

mcqs.question: "The baker made his musical entry on the scene with the 'jhang, jhang' sound of his specially made bamboo staff." What does this show about the pader's place in Goan society?
options: He was a familiar, eagerly awaited friend of every household
He sold bread only during festivals
mcqs.explanation: The musical jingle, the children's rush and the household's welcome show the pader was a loved daily presence, almost a companion.

mcqs.question: Which Coorgi general became the first Chief of the Indian Army?
mcqs.explanation: The text proudly notes that General Cariappa, the first Chief of the Indian Army, was a Coorgi.

mcqs.question: What is the 'second flush' of tea?
options: The sprouting period from May to July that gives the best tea
The second cup of tea at breakfast
mcqs.explanation: Rajvir explains that the second flush or sprouting period lasts from May to July and yields the best tea.

mcqs.question: "The theory of the Arab origin of the Coorgi people draws support from the long, black coat with an embroidered waist-belt worn by them." Which two garments are compared here?
mcqs.explanation: The Kodavus' kuppia resembles the kuffia worn by the Arabs and the Kurds, supporting the Arab-origin theory.

mcqs.question: Which legend of tea's origin involves ten tea plants growing out of eyelids?
options: The legend of Bodhidharma, the Buddhist ascetic who cut off his eyelids
mcqs.explanation: The text says the ascetic Bodhidharma cut off his eyelids to banish sleep during meditation, and ten tea plants grew out of them.

boardQuestions.question: Who were the paders of Goa, and why are they remembered fondly?
boardQuestions.answer: Paders, from the Portuguese word for baker, were the traditional bread-makers of Goa who announced themselves with the jhang, jhang of their bamboo staff. Elders remember them as friends, guides and companions of childhood, and even today the fire in their furnaces has not been extinguished.

boardQuestions.question: What facts about tea did Rajvir share during the train journey?
boardQuestions.answer: Rajvir told Pranjol that over eighty crore cups of tea are drunk every day throughout the world, that the words chai and chini are of Chinese origin, and that tea came to Europe in the sixteenth century and was drunk there more as medicine than as a beverage.

boardQuestions.question: Why was bread indispensable on occasions in Goa? Describe the baker's importance in family celebrations.
boardQuestions.answer: In Goan culture no celebration was complete without bread: marriage gifts were meaningless without the sweet bread called bol, the lady of the house prepared sandwiches on her daughter's engagement, and cakes and bolinhas were a must for Christmas and other festivals. The pader's arrival with loaves, bread bangles and the familiar jingle linked every household to joy and ceremony, making the baker an essential figure in Goan life.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the legends about the discovery of tea as told by Rajvir.
boardQuestions.answer: Rajvir says no one really knows who discovered tea. One Chinese legend tells of an emperor who always boiled water before drinking it; one day a few leaves from a twig burning under the pot fell into it and gave it a delicious flavour. Another legend describes the ancient Buddhist ascetic Bodhidharma, who cut off his eyelids because he felt sleepy during meditation; ten tea plants grew out of them, and their leaves banished sleep.

boardQuestions.question: 'Coorg is a heaven for nature lovers and adventurers.' Describe Coorg with reference to its scenery, people and places worth visiting.
boardQuestions.answer: Coorg or Kodagu, the smallest district of Karnataka, lies midway between Mysore and Mangalore and is home to evergreen rainforests, spices and coffee plantations; the air breathes of invigorating coffee, and the best time to visit is September to March. The river Kaveri takes its water from Coorg's lake and woods; mahaseer fish abound in its waters, kingfishers dive for them, and elephants and mischievous langurs enliven the forests. The people are fiercely brave - the Coorg regiment is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army, General Cariappa was the first Chief of the Indian Army, and the Kodavus are the only community permitted to carry firearms without a licence - and warmly hospitable. Visitors can enjoy the sixty-four-acre island of Nisargadhama, treks to the Brahmagiri hills and the serene Buddhist monks of Bylakuppe.

boardQuestions.question: Compare the attitudes of Rajvir and Pranjol towards the tea gardens during their journey to Assam. Whose attitude do you appreciate and why?
boardQuestions.answer: Rajvir, a Delhi schoolboy, is wide-eyed with wonder: he gazes at the endless sea of tea bushes, tells Pranjol that over eighty crore cups of tea are drunk daily, recounts the Chinese legends of tea and explains that the second flush of May to July yields the finest tea. Pranjol, born and brought up on a tea garden, is surprisingly unmoved; he buries himself in a detective book and finds Rajvir's excitement unnecessary, since familiarity has dulled his curiosity. Rajvir's attitude is more appreciable, because curiosity turns an ordinary journey into learning; those who take their surroundings for granted, like Pranjol, miss the richness of their own heritage. The contrast teaches us to keep a learner's eye on the world.

boardQuestions.question: "Marriage gifts are meaningless without the sweet bread known as the bol. Cakes and bolinhas are a must for Christmas as well as other festivals." Answer the questions that follow: (a) Why was the baker's visit eagerly awaited in every Goan home? (b) How did the baker dress and make his entry? (c) What does the passage show about Goan culture and tradition?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) The passage shows that every happy occasion in Goa needed bread: marriage gifts were meaningless without the bol, engagement sandwiches had to be prepared by the lady of the house, and cakes and bolinhas were a must for Christmas and other festivals, so the baker's visit was eagerly awaited. (b) The baker made a musical entry with the jhang, jhang of his bamboo staff, carrying the basket on his head, and wore the kabai, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees. (c) Though the Portuguese days are gone, the makers still exist; the fire in the furnaces has not been extinguished, showing how tradition survives through family professions.
